## Simple explanation

Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search finds items whose vectors are
similar to a query vector, while trading a small amount of retrieval
accuracy for speed or lower resource use.

## Technical explanation

ANN indexes organize vectors so queries examine only a subset of the
collection. Techniques include graph-based indexes, partitioning and
quantization. Performance is described using measures such as recall at
\(k\), query latency, memory use, and indexing cost. The appropriate
trade-off depends on the application and its data.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Embedding-based search and retrieval-augmented generation often need to
retrieve from large vector collections. ANN can make these searches
practical at scale, but approximate results should be measured against the
application's relevance and latency requirements.

## How it works

An index is built from the stored vectors. At query time, the index uses
its structure to visit promising candidates, computes or refines distances
for those candidates, and returns the best matches it found. Search
parameters can trade additional work for higher recall.

## Practical example

A document-search service embeds a user's question and uses an ANN index to
retrieve a short list of semantically similar document chunks for a later
ranking or generation step.

## Common misconceptions

- ANN does not guarantee the mathematically exact nearest items.
- High vector similarity does not necessarily mean a result is useful or
  factually relevant.
- Index choice involves build time, memory, updates, and recall, not only
  query speed.
